newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG to protest to Australia over contact with rebels.
newsitem.headline: PNG to protest to Australia over contact with rebels.

text.p: Papua New Guinea Prime Minister John Giheno said on Tuesday he would protest to Australia over reports he allowed two lawyers acting as freelance Australian diplomats to meet secessionist rebels.

The South Pacific nation's caretaker leader said reports he had given permission for the pair to pass through a military blockade to meet Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) leaders on Bougainville island were "blatant lies".

He said in a statement his department would write to the Australian High Commission in Port Moresby to "protest in the strongest possible terms (against) their continued obsession with our domestic affairs".

One of the lawers on Tuesday confirmed the pair had gone to Bougainville, 800 kilometres (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby, to negotiate with all parties in the nine-year conflict in a bid to bring in international negotiators.

Lawyer Mark Plunkett said the pair were trying to encourage the warring parties to take part in a joint negotiation training project to be conducted by the Harvard Law School's conflict management group.

Plunkett, a former U.N. special prosecutor in Cambodia, denied he and colleague Leo White received permission from Giheno, or that they were compiling a report for Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
"In this project we are neutral and impartial," he said.
"My colleague and I do not act at the behest of the Australian, PNG or any other government, nor are we bound to report to the Australian, PNG or any other government."
Australian sources familiar with the plan have previously confirmed Canberra had offered to fund the Harvard project.
A spokesman for Downer was not be immediately available for comment on Tuesday.

An Australian media report, carried by newspapers in Port Moresby, said Giheno had allowed Plunkett and White -- described as "freelance diplomats" -- had allowed the two lawyers through the blockade to meet rebel leaders and would report to Downer.
Giheno also accused Australia of failing to give adequate support to Port Moresby in ending the Bougainville crisis.
"They have hesitated to make a firm commitment to Bougainville but cry foul every time we have turned elsewhere for help," Giheno said.

Giheno was appointed acting prime minister last month after Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan was forced to stand aside by a military mutiny and civil protests over a plan to use African mercenaries to quell the Bougainville rebellion.
Australia, Papua New Guinea's former colonial ruler, has close diplomatic, security and business ties with Port Moresby.
Canberra has previously hosted several rounds of talks that failed to bring peace to the resource rich island.
